paragraphs: Conformal regression builds prediction regions intended to contain the true outcome at a specified coverage level. Predicting several outputs together is harder because their dependencies affect the region’s shape, and constructing that region can be computationally expensive. This paper brings nine methods into a common framework to clarify their properties and relationships.

The authors also introduce two families of conformity scores, the quantities used to decide which candidate outcomes belong in a prediction region. One works with any generative model. The other uses invertible generative models to make computation more efficient. Both extend ideas previously used for single-output regression.

The coverage claims distinguish two different guarantees: exact marginal coverage with finite samples, and conditional coverage asymptotically. The latter concerns coverage given the input and is not asserted as an exact finite-sample guarantee. An evaluation on 13 tabular datasets uses one shared code base, making comparisons more consistent. The contribution combines a common basis for evaluating existing methods with new scores that offer different modeling and computational choices.
icml-2025-a-unified-comparative-study-wi.tldr: A unified comparison of multi-output conformal regression introduces two score families combining finite-sample marginal coverage with asymptotic conditional coverage.

paragraphs: An AI teammate needs to coordinate with people whose behavior it may not already know. Hanabi makes this challenge concrete: players cooperate despite incomplete information and limited communication, and successful actions depend on interpreting teammates’ intentions. Evaluating such coordination directly with humans, however, is costly and difficult to reproduce.

The paper introduces the Ad-Hoc Human-AI Coordination Challenge, which uses learned human proxy agents as evaluation partners. These agents are developed from a large human gameplay dataset and are intended to provide inexpensive, reproducible, human-like interactions. This gives researchers a consistent setting for comparing how well their agents cooperate with such partners.

The challenge releases 3,079 games, deliberately restricting available human data to encourage methods that learn efficiently. It also supplies baseline results for two-player and three-player Hanabi. The proxy agents remain behind a controlled evaluation system to support fair comparisons. The central contribution is an evaluation setup that makes human-oriented coordination research more repeatable while retaining the game’s demands for communication, inference, and joint action.
icml-2025-ad-hoc-human-ai-coordination-c.tldr: AH2AC2 uses learned human proxy partners to make evaluation of human-AI coordination in Hanabi cheaper and more reproducible.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression when only an unknown minority of data batches are trustworthy. A clean batch contains independent samples from the target regression distribution; the other batches can be arbitrary. The algorithm must return a short list of candidate regression vectors, with at least one close to the true vector.

The new method uses higher-order information about the covariates, under the assumption that their moments have bounds certifiable through Sum-of-Squares reasoning. It combines that framework with an iterative procedure and a new way to prune candidate lists. For any fixed positive delta, the minimum batch size scales as alpha to the minus delta, where alpha is the clean fraction.

The method achieves error proportional to alpha to the minus delta over two, divided by the square root of batch size, and an optimal list size of order one over alpha. Smaller delta requires higher-degree moment assumptions and increases the polynomial resource requirements. These conditional guarantees improve batch size, error, and list size over the earlier result. The paper also supplies a Sum-of-Squares proof of a moment inequality that may have broader uses.
icml-2025-batch-list-decodable-linear-re.tldr: With certifiably bounded higher moments, a new regression algorithm tolerates mostly corrupted batches while improving batch size, error, and candidate-list guarantees.

paragraphs: Routing systems try to reduce language-model costs by assigning each query to a model with a suitable balance of price and quality. When the router considers only one response per model, a small model may appear inadequate. This can push too many queries toward an expensive model, even when another use of the smaller model could work.

BEST-Route expands the routing decision to include how many responses to generate. Sampling several answers from a small model and selecting the best can improve quality while still costing less than one answer from a large model. The framework chooses both the model and its sample count using query difficulty and quality thresholds.

Experiments on real-world datasets report cost reductions of up to 60% with less than a 1% performance drop. These are reported experimental outcomes, rather than a guarantee for every query. The result shows why routing and response sampling are useful to consider together: additional computation on a cheaper model can sometimes provide a better cost-quality tradeoff than switching models.
icml-2025-best-route-adaptive-llm-routin.tldr: BEST-Route jointly chooses a language model and response sample count, reporting up to 60% lower costs with less than 1% performance loss.

paragraphs: Tree ensembles combine predictions from multiple decision trees and can offer strong predictive performance. Their size matters beyond storage: checking properties such as fairness or robustness can have a cost that grows exponentially with ensemble size. Smaller ensembles can also reduce energy consumption when deployed on battery-powered devices.

The paper proposes Level-wise Optimization and Pruning, or LOP, to compress an existing ensemble. It can prune parts of trees or remove whole trees. Alongside these structural changes, it adjusts the predictions stored at the remaining leaves so that predictive accuracy is mostly preserved. Compression therefore involves both reducing the structure and updating what the surviving structure predicts.

The empirical results report compression factors often 10 to 100 times better than those achieved by competing methods. This compares compression factors, rather than claiming the same numerical improvement in accuracy, energy use, or verification time. The work matters because it directly targets ensemble size while largely retaining predictive behavior, addressing a practical obstacle for verification and resource-constrained deployment.
icml-2025-compressing-tree-ensembles-thr.tldr: LOP compresses tree ensembles through pruning and leaf-prediction updates, with empirically much stronger compression factors while mostly preserving accuracy.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships without interventions often requires restrictive assumptions to identify a unique causal structure. When those assumptions fail, the associated guarantees can disappear. Earlier work on two variables suggested that Bayesian model selection could replace restrictive modeling assumptions with more flexible ones, accepting a small probability of error.

This paper extends that approach to multiple variables. It uses a Bayesian nonparametric model called the Causal Gaussian Process Conditional Density Estimator. The model’s hyperparameters define an adjacency matrix, which represents proposed relationships between variables. A continuous relaxation makes it possible to optimize this representation instead of handling model selection solely as a discrete search.

The optimization combines marginal likelihood with an acyclicity regularizer and returns a maximum a posteriori causal graph. The regularizer encourages a graph without directed cycles, while the Bayesian criterion guides selection among models. The authors report competitive performance, supporting Bayesian selection as a useful multivariate approach. The result favors more flexible assumptions and probabilistic model selection rather than establishing assumption-free, error-free causal identification.
icml-2025-continuous-bayesian-model-sele.tldr: A continuous Bayesian model-selection method extends flexible causal discovery to multiple variables and reports competitive performance.

paragraphs: The task is to estimate the mean of a high-dimensional Gaussian when some samples come from Gaussians centered elsewhere. The clean distribution and contaminating distributions all have identity covariance. Fewer than half the samples are contaminated in the model, but the contaminating means are unknown and can be arbitrary.

This structure makes mean-shift contamination different from unrestricted adversarial contamination. Previous work established that the target mean can be estimated consistently under mean shifts. However, the known robust estimators required running time exponential in the dimension, leaving a gap between what the data permit statistically and what algorithms could achieve efficiently.

The paper gives the first computationally efficient algorithm for this high-dimensional setting that tolerates a constant fraction of outliers. It uses a near-optimal number of samples, runs in time polynomial in that sample count, and can achieve any desired accuracy. The contribution depends on the specified Gaussian contamination structure. It demonstrates that a noise model allowing arbitrary shifts while retaining shared covariance can support both strong statistical accuracy and computational efficiency.
icml-2025-efficient-multivariate-robust-.tldr: A new algorithm efficiently estimates a high-dimensional Gaussian mean to arbitrary accuracy under structured mean-shift contamination.

paragraphs: Multi-step decisions require assessing how an action contributes to an eventual objective. Language models can struggle when actions are generated with a short-term focus, while approaches based on simulated futures also depend on the quality of those simulations and evaluations. This paper introduces LAC, an actor-critic framework for improving language-model policies using longer-term action assessments.

The critic computes Q-values, estimates of an action’s value, from token logits associated with positive and negative outcomes. Future trajectory rollouts and reasoning enrich these evaluations. A gradient-free policy-improvement mechanism then uses the assessments to improve decisions, providing a way to combine the model’s knowledge with structured action evaluation.

Experiments cover ALFWorld, BabyAI-Text, and WebShop, spanning high-level decisions, low-level actions, and large action spaces. The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art methods and competitive results with models containing seven or eight billion parameters. On complex tasks, these models even outperform baseline methods using GPT-4. The findings support the usefulness of long-term evaluation and policy improvement across the tested decision environments.
icml-2025-enhancing-decision-making-of-l.tldr: LAC combines language-model action evaluations, future rollouts, and gradient-free policy improvement to strengthen multi-step decision-making.

paragraphs: Long-context attention is expensive even though only a small subset of tokens may contribute strongly to a particular output. The challenge is finding those tokens cheaply. The paper formulates that search as maximum inner product search, while identifying problems with existing methods: poor GPU compatibility and difficulty handling the different distributions of queries and keys.

HashAttention learns mappings that turn queries and keys into binary representations in Hamming space. It treats token selection like recommending relevant items for a query. Fast bitwise comparisons identify promising tokens, and attention is then computed only over that subset. The additional representation requires 32 bits of auxiliary memory per token.

With generic training data, the method reduces the number of attended tokens by up to 16 times with minimal quality loss; task-specific fine-tuning enables 32-fold sparsity. At that sparsity on an A100 GPU, reported attention speedups reach 4.3 times in GPT-FAST and 2.54 times in FlashDecode. GPT-FAST throughput improves by up to 3.12 times, showing practical benefits beyond reducing token counts.
icml-2025-hashattention-semantic-sparsit.tldr: HashAttention uses learned binary representations to select important tokens efficiently, reducing attention work with minimal reported quality loss.

paragraphs: Federated learning must fit both network communication budgets and the computing limits of participating devices. Quantization can reduce the number of bits used to represent training quantities, but existing approaches do not simultaneously address both communication directions and client computation. LBI-FL targets all three by quantizing weights, activations, and gradients below eight-bit integer precision.

The framework uses reinforcement learning to adjust bit widths over the course of training. Its agent considers information including current precision, training stage, and quantization loss. The authors report that an agent trained efficiently on small datasets transfers to different network architectures and datasets whose distributions vary across clients.

The theoretical analysis establishes a convergence rate equivalent to FedAvg for federated learning with gradient quantization. The framework can reduce communication costs eightfold relative to full-precision federated learning. Experiments also report an average reduction of more than 50% in client bit operations, with less than 2% accuracy loss compared with eight-bit training. These results use different comparison points for communication and computation, highlighting the framework’s combined efficiency goals.
icml-2025-lbi-fl-low-bit-integerized-fed.tldr: LBI-FL dynamically assigns sub-eight-bit precision during federated training to reduce communication and client computation while largely preserving accuracy.

paragraphs: Training procedures often let each example or federated client contribute to only part of the overall computation. This paper studies how randomness in that participation can strengthen privacy guarantees. It considers both data partitioning, where participation covers selected iterations, and model partitioning, where contributions update selected parameters.

For federated model parallelism, each client updates a randomly chosen subnetwork to save memory and computation. The authors show that techniques such as model splitting and dropout also provide significant privacy amplification that earlier analyses did not capture. The contribution is partly analytical: existing training randomness can offer privacy gains beyond those recognized by previous accounting methods.

The paper also introduces balanced iteration subsampling, which gives each example or client a fixed number of participating iterations. In certain regimes, this produces stronger privacy amplification than independently sampling participation with a Poisson scheme. The broader finding is that useful privacy randomness need not be independent across training steps. Structured participation patterns, including those that interact with model parameters, can be analyzed systematically.
icml-2025-leveraging-randomness-in-model.tldr: Structured randomness in training participation can amplify privacy, with balanced iteration subsampling outperforming Poisson sampling in certain regimes.

paragraphs: Map-based reasoning involves more than recognizing a place name. A model may need to compare distances, follow directions, plan a route, or combine information from map tools. MapEval is designed to test these capabilities across textual reasoning, API interactions, and visual map analysis, including tasks that require handling long contexts.

The benchmark contains 700 multiple-choice questions covering 180 cities in 54 countries. Its questions address spatial relationships, navigation, travel planning, and interactions with real-world maps. This scope connects several forms of input and tool use within one evaluation, allowing researchers to examine geospatial reasoning beyond simple location queries.

Across 30 evaluated foundation models, none exceeds 67% accuracy. The authors report substantially worse performance from open-source models and a gap of more than 20% behind human performance for every tested model. Difficulties include distances, directions, route planning, and reasoning about particular places. These findings identify weaknesses in the evaluated models’ ability to turn map information into correct answers, despite broader progress in reasoning and autonomous tool use.
icml-2025-mapeval-a-map-based-evaluation.tldr: MapEval tests geospatial reasoning through text, APIs, and maps, finding substantial gaps between 30 foundation models and human performance.

paragraphs: Maximum entropy reinforcement learning rewards both task success and diversity in action selection, encouraging exploration and policy robustness. A common implementation, Soft Actor-Critic, uses a Gaussian policy. The paper identifies that policy’s single-mode structure as a constraint in complex environments with multiple goals, where useful behavior may require a more varied action distribution.

MaxEntDP replaces that policy representation with a diffusion model, which can capture distributions with multiple modes. The method uses this expressive representation to pursue the maximum entropy objective. The authors state that it enables efficient exploration and brings the learned policy closer to the optimal policy for that objective.

On MuJoCo benchmarks, MaxEntDP outperforms Gaussian policies and other generative models evaluated within the maximum entropy framework. It also performs comparably to other state-of-the-art diffusion-based online reinforcement-learning algorithms. These findings support the choice of policy representation as an important part of exploration: a richer distribution can better accommodate multiple promising behaviors while remaining part of an entropy-encouraging learning objective.
icml-2025-maximum-entropy-reinforcement-.tldr: MaxEntDP uses a diffusion policy for maximum entropy reinforcement learning, improving exploration and outperforming tested Gaussian-policy alternatives on MuJoCo.

paragraphs: Preference-based learning can be manipulated when an adversary changes which option is labeled preferable. This paper studies that problem in contextual dueling bandits, where decisions depend on context and feedback compares options. The corruption model allows an adversary to flip preference labels during learning.

The proposed RCDB algorithm uses uncertainty-weighted maximum likelihood estimation. Up to logarithmic factors, its regret bound scales as d times the square root of T divided by kappa, plus d times C divided by kappa. Here d is context dimension, T is the number of rounds, C counts corrupted feedback, and kappa bounds the link function’s derivative from below. A matching lower-bound analysis establishes near-optimality both with and without corruption.

For a sigmoid link, a further algorithm uses refined estimates of local derivatives to remove kappa dependence from the leading term in T. This changes exponential dependence on the parameter radius into polynomial dependence. Experiments with different adversarial feedback patterns report RCDB outperforming state-of-the-art dueling-bandit methods. Together, the theory and evaluation characterize how learning degrades as corrupted feedback increases.
icml-2025-nearly-optimal-algorithms-for-.tldr: RCDB learns from adversarially corrupted preference feedback with nearly optimal regret, while a sigmoid-specific refinement improves parameter dependence.

paragraphs: Functional MRI can represent relationships among brain regions as a network. Existing graph neural networks can extract features from these networks, but the paper argues that they often miss complex relationships involving brain regions and demographic information. NeuroTree is designed to capture richer organization in functional networks associated with mental disorders.

The framework combines a k-hop AGE-GCN, neural ordinary differential equations, and contrastive masked functional connectivity. These components help represent similarities and differences in distances between brain regions. NeuroTree then decodes the network features into trees, providing a hierarchical representation of regional pathways and neural behavioral patterns.

The tree representation is intended to capture higher-order relationships useful for understanding disease-related subnetworks. Across two mental-disorder datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and insights into age-related deterioration patterns and their neural mechanisms. The work’s contribution combines predictive feature learning with a structured representation of brain-network organization. Its reported findings concern the evaluated datasets and the patterns revealed by that representation, tying performance improvements to an effort to understand hierarchical functional pathways.
icml-2025-neurotree-hierarchical-functio.tldr: NeuroTree converts functional brain-network features into hierarchical trees and reports state-of-the-art results on two mental-disorder datasets.

paragraphs: When several servers each hold a set of items, estimating the total number of distinct items requires accounting for overlap. The goal is an estimate within a multiplicative factor of one plus epsilon while exchanging as few bits as possible. This paper asks how communication changes when overlap is limited.

The authors parameterize difficulty by pairwise collisions: occurrences of the same element across servers. Their protocol has a communication term that depends on the square root of a rescaled collision count, alongside a term reflecting the number of servers and universe size. This yields improved communication when collisions are few, identifying easier instances within a problem with established worst-case bounds.

Further improvements use assumptions about the number of distinct items or collisions, and matching lower bounds establish collision count as a tight complexity measure across the studied regimes. The paper also examines streaming estimation using the number of items appearing more than once. The results explain how instance structure can make a counting task substantially easier than its worst-case communication requirements suggest.
icml-2025-on-fine-grained-distinct-eleme.tldr: Collision-sensitive algorithms and matching lower bounds explain when distributed distinct counting needs less communication than worst-case bounds suggest.

paragraphs: Learning a mixture of Gaussian distributions can become prohibitively difficult as the number of components grows. One way to seek tractable cases is to assume all components share an unknown covariance and no component has exponentially small weight. Earlier work gave a quasi-polynomial-time algorithm for this structured family.

This paper shows that the earlier upper bound is essentially best possible within the Statistical Query model, even when every component has the same weight. Its lower bound applies to distinguishing such a mixture from a standard Gaussian. Thus, uniform weights alone do not eliminate the computational obstacle, even for a testing task rather than full mixture recovery.

The authors then examine what happens when most weights are uniform but a small fraction may be arbitrary. They give a quasi-polynomial upper bound for the same testing problem in this setting. Together, the results clarify both a hardness boundary and a tractable extension: substantial weight regularity still leaves Statistical Query difficulty, while limited departures from uniformity can preserve the stated testing-time guarantee.
icml-2025-on-learning-parallel-pancakes-.tldr: Uniform Gaussian-mixture weights still permit Statistical Query hardness, while mostly uniform weights admit a quasi-polynomial testing algorithm.

paragraphs: LLaMA-Adapter uses zero-initialized attention as an efficient fine-tuning mechanism intended to stabilize training and improve performance. Although the technique has empirical support, the paper identifies a gap in its theoretical explanation. The authors study how its prompts and gating functions can be estimated.

Their analysis connects zero-initialized attention to mixture-of-experts models, giving a framework for examining the prompt components and the gates that control their contribution. They prove optimal estimation results for both linear and nonlinear prompts, along with gating functions. Nonlinear prompts provide greater flexibility within this analysis, motivating their use beyond the linear form.

Experiments on open language-model benchmarks support the theoretical investigation: nonlinear prompts outperform linear prompts in the reported evaluations. Both forms consistently outperform vanilla attention even with limited training data. These findings give the work two complementary contributions: a mathematical account of estimating the adaptation components, and empirical evidence that the more flexible prompt form improves performance. The limited-data results also support the authors’ claims about the method’s robustness and adaptability.
icml-2025-on-zero-initialized-attention-.tldr: A mixture-of-experts analysis establishes optimal prompt and gate estimation for zero-initialized attention, with experiments favoring nonlinear prompts.

paragraphs: In this online classification problem, an adversary chooses the inputs, but labels are constrained by Massart noise: each observed label differs from its ground truth with an unknown probability at most eta. The paper focuses on linear classifiers with a gamma margin, combining difficult input selection with bounded label corruption.

The authors give the first computationally efficient algorithm with a mistake bound of eta times T plus a term that grows more slowly than T. Over many rounds, the extra mistakes per round therefore vanish. The result is qualitatively tight for efficient algorithms under standard complexity assumptions, because even offline learning cannot efficiently guarantee classification error below eta.

The paper extends the approach to contextual bandits with k actions. Expected rewards need only respect a linear ranking, with a gap of at least Delta whenever one action ranks above another. Using the online learner, the bandit algorithm exceeds random action selection in expected total reward by at least (1 minus one over k) times Delta times T, minus a sublinear term.
icml-2025-online-linear-classification-w.tldr: An efficient online classifier reaches a qualitatively tight Massart-noise mistake bound and supports a bandit algorithm under linear reward-ranking assumptions.

paragraphs: Language-model watermarks embed detectable signals in generated content using a secret key. Robustness means that removing detectability should require a significant loss of content quality. The paper argues that testing only attackers who do not adapt to the watermarking method can give an incomplete picture of this property.

The authors express watermark robustness as an optimization objective and use preference-based optimization to tune attacks to particular watermarking methods. Their evaluation therefore examines attackers that actively improve against the defense being tested. The resulting paraphrasers provide a way to study how watermark detection behaves under this more targeted pressure.

In the reported evaluation, adaptive attacks evade every surveyed watermark. Training against any evaluated watermark also produces attacks that evade unseen watermarks, and the optimization-based attacks are reported to be cost-effective. These findings concern the surveyed methods and tested attacks, rather than establishing failure for every possible watermark. The central implication is that robustness assessments should include adaptively tuned attackers, because success against non-adaptive attacks can leave meaningful vulnerabilities undiscovered.
icml-2025-optimizing-adaptive-attacks-ag.tldr: Adaptively optimized paraphrasing attacks evade all surveyed language-model watermarks and transfer to unseen watermarks in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Many diffusion models for three-dimensional molecules use specialized networks that handle rotations and translations through built-in equivariance. These architectures have produced strong samples, but their specialized structure can limit efficiency and scalability. This paper explores a way to relax those architectural constraints while still accounting for molecular orientation.

The method learns a separate rotation for each molecule, creating an aligned latent representation. It then trains a non-equivariant diffusion model on those aligned representations. The key design choice is to handle orientation through learned alignment before generation in latent space, allowing the diffusion network itself to operate without the same equivariance requirements.

Experiments show significantly better performance than previously reported non-equivariant models. Sample quality is comparable to state-of-the-art equivariant diffusion models, while training and sampling become more efficient. These findings support learned rotational alignment as a practical alternative for the tested molecule-generation setting. The contribution links representation design to computational flexibility: organizing the latent space can reduce the burden placed on specialized generative architectures.
icml-2025-scalable-non-equivariant-3d-mo.tldr: Learned molecular rotations enable non-equivariant diffusion with sample quality comparable to leading equivariant models and improved training and sampling efficiency.

paragraphs: Learning the geometry of a data manifold means describing the lower-dimensional structure along which the data vary. The challenge is to make both learning that structure and computing with it efficient. This paper combines generative modeling with pullback Riemannian geometry in a score-based framework, focusing initially on unimodal distributions.

The proposed geometric structure has closed-form geodesics, or geometry-respecting paths, that pass through the data probability density. The authors use it to construct a Riemannian autoencoder with error bounds for discovering the manifold’s correct dimension. They also connect the framework to anisotropic normalizing flows through an isometry regularizer used during training.

Numerical experiments, including image datasets, produce high-quality paths through the data support and reliable estimates of intrinsic dimension. The framework also supplies a global chart, a coordinate description covering the manifold. These results connect efficient path computation, dimension estimation, and coordinate construction in one approach. The stated focus on unimodal distributions defines the initial scope of this attempt to extract a manifold’s complete geometry.
icml-2025-score-based-pullback-riemannia.tldr: A score-based geometric framework provides closed-form geodesics, manifold coordinates, and dimension estimation, initially focusing on unimodal distributions.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear classification when there are multiple labels and random label corruption follows a known matrix. Inputs come from an unknown distribution. The noise matrix specifies how likely each true class is to become another observed class, and its separation parameter compares keeping the correct label with individual incorrect alternatives.

For two labels, earlier algorithms can achieve optimal error in polynomial time. The authors show a sharp change within the Statistical Query model once there are three labels. Even with constant noise separation, achieving optimal error requires super-polynomial Statistical Query complexity. Knowing the corruption matrix therefore does not remove this computational barrier.

With more labels and smaller separation, the lower bounds become stronger: they also obstruct obtaining any constant-factor approximation to optimal loss, or even improving on a trivial hypothesis. These are lower bounds for Statistical Query algorithms, so their scope is a specified computational model. The findings show why efficient methods for noisy binary classification cannot automatically be expected to extend to the multiclass setting.
icml-2025-statistical-query-hardness-of-.tldr: Statistical Query lower bounds reveal a sharp increase in noisy linear-classification difficulty when moving from two labels to three or more.

paragraphs: Combining several models often improves generalization in classical settings, but modern overparameterized ensembles may offer little advantage over a single larger model. This paper investigates that difference through random-feature regression. The aim is to understand when the familiar benefits of averaging models change as model capacity grows.

The authors prove, under minimal assumptions, that infinite ensembles of overparameterized random-feature regressors produce the same pointwise predictions as a single infinite-width regressor. Finite-width ensembles rapidly approach single models with the same total parameter budget. These relationships are exact without ridge regularization and approximate when ridge penalties are small, implying nearly identical generalization in the analyzed setting.

The paper also characterizes disagreement among ensemble members. In this framework, predictive variance measures the expected effects of adding capacity rather than a conventional notion of uncertainty. Together, the results challenge transferring classical ensemble intuitions directly to overparameterized models. Random-feature regression supplies the theoretical basis for that challenge; the findings motivate reconsideration of deep ensembles without claiming an unrestricted equivalence theorem for all neural networks.
icml-2025-theoretical-limitations-of-ens.tldr: For overparameterized random-feature regression, ensembles approach single models with matching parameter budgets, challenging familiar generalization and uncertainty intuitions.

paragraphs: Searching for images or videos using text can fail when visual content contains distracting detail or represents information at a different level of specificity from the query. This paper introduces VISA, a test-time method for addressing both problems. It uses existing large models to convert visual content into textual descriptions.

Those descriptions concentrate semantic information and filter out low-level visual redundancy. VISA then adds a question-answering process to refine the descriptions with details at the granularity requested by the user. The approach therefore combines a general textual abstraction of the content with information tailored to what the query is asking.

Experiments report substantial improvements in both image and video retrieval, across short and long queries. Because the method operates at test time, the authors position it as a plug-and-play addition to existing retrieval systems. The contribution is a way to improve matching through the representation used during retrieval: descriptions emphasize meaning, while query-guided questions help align the level of detail between the request and the visual content.
icml-2025-visual-abstraction-a-plug-and-.tldr: VISA improves image and video retrieval at test time by generating textual descriptions and refining them with query-specific questions.
